To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the alert period for influenza hospitalizations was longer than the alert period for laboratory positive tests.
the influenza alert created from the laboratory data was able to provide a pre-peak warning of influenza hospitalizations at a regional level.

(1) the laboratory-based indicator of influenza activity (FluWatch) was a good predictor of influenza hospitalizations in Canada; (2) it provided a pre-peak warning of 3 weeks in most seasons and (3) the difference in timing between the two indicators was not significant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of how to evaluate an indicator of influenza activity.
the development of a statistical model for the prediction of influenza activity.
the development of an alert system based on laboratory data and hospitalization records.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the laboratory data is an adequate indicator of influenza activity, but not a perfect one.

laboratory positive tests were a good indicator of the influenza activity at the regional level, but that the timing of the alerts relative to the influenza hospitalizations was variable and unpredictable.
the laboratory data was a good indicator but the difference in timing was small and not significant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
laboratory data can serve as a good indicator of the timing of influenza activity and can provide a reasonable pre-epidemic alert at the regional level.
the evaluation of an indicator for influenza epidemics should not be restricted to internal criteria.
the evaluation of an indicator for influenza epidemics requires a multi-faceted approach that considers both internal and external criteria.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of indicator for influenza should be guided by its ability to predict influenza hospitalizations, rather than by internal criteria.
the evaluation of candidate indicators should include external criteria, such as lead/lag timing, in order to ensure the indicator is appropriate for its intended purpose.
cross-validation of the performance of an epidemic indicator is essential.
